info.bio:
Grupo de pop-rock originario de Londres, UK  formado en 1989 y disuelto en 2003. Su nombre lo tomaron de la canción Suedehead de Morrissey. En EE.UU. fueron conocidos como The London Suede, puesto que su nombre original ya estaba registrado.

La formación con la que se dieron a conocer fue: Brett Anderson (Voz), Bernard Butler (Guitarra), Matt Osman (Bajo) y Simon Gilbert (Batería). Antes de grabar su primer disco también pasaron por la banda fugazmente el batería de The Smiths

scenes.name: Brit-pop y post-pop
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Como tantas veces, el fenómeno más publicitado es el menos interesante: un «brit-pop» de grupos terriblemente parecidos y tediosos, sin apenas imaginación. Lo anticipan Lightning Seeds, La's, Teenage Fanclub y Heavenly; estalla con Boo Radleys, Blur (Parklife) y Oasis (el «farol» que mejor personifica la moda). Suede y el glam-pop (Super Furry Animals, Placebo), las excepciones de High Llamas (Hawaii) y Supergrass, el revival mod (Ocean Colour Scene, Wildhearts), Elastica, Sleeper, las Spice Girls; Trembling Blue Stars, Tindersticks, Delgados. El post-pop de Radiohead, «la banda más publicitada y sobrevalorada de la década», cuyo OK Computer es una obra maestra del falso vanguardismo; Coldplay, Travis.

If nothing else, Suede (1), featuring guitarist Bernard Butler and vocalist Brett Anderson, offered an original take on glam-pop on Suede (1993), one that inspired bands such as the Super Furry Animals, with Fuzzy Logic (1996), and Placebo , with Placebo (1996). The Smiths were a…

podcast.title: Early Relevance (1991)
podcast.body: By 1991, two years before their debut album, Suede was already an "important and relevant" band in the UK, amidst a significant "hunger for musical novelties" alongside the emergence of Blur. They gained significant magazine exposure with only a couple of singles of "small repercussion." "Swade ya era una banda importante y relevante dentro del Reino Unido."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Early Britpop Appearance (1992)
podcast.body: Suede is credited with the "very first science" of what would become Britpop, appearing in 1992 and actively rejecting the prevailing grunge trend in the UK. Instead, they celebrated eccentric English rock from earlier decades. "The very first science of what we would eventually call Britpop appeared in 1992 with a band called Swade."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop

podcast.title: Early Britpop Appearance (1992)
podcast.body: Suede appeared in 1992, at a time when most of the UK was enamored with grunge. The band, however, rejected grunge, choosing instead to celebrate a distinctly British sound. "The very first science of what we would eventually call Britpop appeared in 1992 with a band called Swade."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Cover Story on Select Magazine - April 1993
podcast.body: The April 1993 issue of Select magazine, which became a mouthpiece for Britpop, featured Suede's Brett Anderson on the cover with the headline "Yanks Go Home." This solidified their role in the burgeoning movement against American music dominance. "The April 1993 issue featured Swade's Brit Anderson on the cover next to a headline that read, Yanks Go Home."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: Dominant British Bands (End of 1994)
podcast.body: By the end of 1994, Suede was one of three bands dominating the British music scene, alongside Oasis and Blur, indicating an impending explosion in the Britpop movement. "As we got to the end of 1994, three bands dominated the British music scene. There was Oasis, there was Blur, and there was Swade."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop

podcast.title: Artwork Designer
podcast.body: Peter Saville, chief art design guy at Factory Records, did design work for Suede. "He did everything from gig posters to album design for Joy Division New Order, Roxas music, Swade, pulp, Martha Nemuffins, and Noam D."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bernard Butler's Mysterious Exit
podcast.body: During the recording of *Dog Man Star*, Bernard Butler, a key musical contributor to the success of Suede's first album, abruptly abandoned the band. His departure was unusual, with his belongings reportedly found outside the studio and him being denied entry, indicating a sudden and acrimonious split. "Bernard Butler... acababa abandonando la banda, además de esa manera tan rara."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Bowie's Appreciation for Suede
podcast.body: David Bowie was a known fan of Suede, acknowledging their importance in the alt-rock era. This mutual respect between Bowie and the new generation of musicians highlighted his continued relevance. "Knowing that Bowie was a fan of the pixies and Irvana and the smashing pumpkins and swayed and a wasis and blur and vice versa, you had to give him respect."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Brett Anderson's Dandy English Pop Persona
podcast.body: Singer Brett Anderson adopted the persona of a "dandy English pop" figure, proudly singing in a London accent and actively contrasting Suede's style with grunge. "And singer Brett Anderson played up the part of the dandy English pop, proudly singing in a London accent."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop

podcast.title: Brett Anderson's Reputation and Struggles
podcast.body: Following *Dog Man Star*, Suede faced a challenging period marked by Brett Anderson's severe heroin addiction, which significantly complicated touring and creative work. The band experienced continued lineup changes and internal strife, with Anderson gaining a reputation as a "despot" within the group. "Bret Anderson siempre tuvo fama de ser un auténtico les potado dentro de la banda."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Brit-Pop Avant-garde
podcast.body: Suede is considered to have been at the forefront of the Brit-pop movement, which began almost simultaneously with the Grunge movement around 1989. "Justo en 1989 casi a la vez arrancaba el movimiento Britop posiblemente con sweat, que era un poco la avanza dilla."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: La generación perdida del Indie: SHOEGAZE

podcast.title: Britpop Movement (Mid-to-Late 90s)
podcast.body: Suede was a key band in the Britpop movement, which was a British response to American Grunge. "the British were still ringing out what they could from Britpop...you know Oasis and Blur and Elastakund swayed in all those bands."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Britpop Revolution Kickstart
podcast.body: Suede is credited with kickstarting the Britpop revolution of the 1990s, offering short, sharp guitar-based pop songs infused with British slang and eccentricities. They represented a homegrown alternative to American grunge. "Swade, the band really kickstarted the brick pop revolution of the 1990s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: Britpop's First Couple Connection
podcast.body: Justine Frischmann, a member of Elastica and Damon Albarn's girlfriend, was also a former member of Suede and a former girlfriend of Brett Anderson. This interconnectedness was highlighted by the British music media. "Not only was she a former member of swayed, but she was also a former girlfriend of Brent Anderson of swayed, and Damon Albarn's Kurt girlfriend."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Celebration of English Rock Traditions
podcast.body: Suede, notably singer Brett Anderson, consciously celebrated great eccentric English rock of the 70s and 80s, drawing influences from artists like Bowie, Roxy Music, T-Rex, The Smiths, and Morrissey, incorporating British psych and "Jagger swagger" with glam guitars. "Instead, Swade celebrated the great eccentric English rock of the 70s and 80s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop

podcast.title: Critical Acclaim Before Debut
podcast.body: Suede achieved the rare feat of being featured on magazine covers (such as Melody Maker in April 1991, with the headline "The Best New Band in Britain") and being invited to perform at awards ceremonies before they had even released a single album. Esteemed figures like Morrissey and Siouxsie referenced Suede's potential in interviews in 1991. They performed as an "emerging band" at the Express music awards in January 1991. "llegó a ser portadas de revistas musicales en el Reino Unido sin ni siquiera haber tenido un solo disco."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Critical Acclaim in the Early 90s
podcast.body: In the early 1990s, particularly around the time of Blur's "Modern Life Is Rubbish," critics were highly enthusiastic about Suede's work, giving their records a great deal of positive recognition for doing quite distinct things musically.

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Early 1990s Glam Revival
podcast.body: Suede, emerging in the early 1990s, immediately displayed clear influences from David Bowie, Roxy Music, and the broader glam rock movement, showing glam's continued presence. "When they showed up in the early 1990s, it took all of two seconds to understand that they were equal parts Bowie, Roxy, and Glam."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

podcast.title: Early Britpop Signifier
podcast.body: Suede appeared in 1992, at a time when most of the UK was enamored with grunge. The band, however, rejected grunge, choosing instead to celebrate a distinctly British sound. "The very first science of what we would eventually call Britpop appeared in 1992 with a band called Swade."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Foppish Fashion and Glam Rock Influence
podcast.body: Unlike grunge bands, Suede embraced a foppish fashion sense. Singer Brett Anderson was a fan of David Bowie's glam rock period from the early 1970s, which by 1992, sounded fresh again. "Swade came with a sense of foppish fashion. Singer Brett Anderson was a fan of David Bowie's glam rock period of the early 1970s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: Formation and Early Recognition
podcast.body: A group of "precocious university students," influenced by artists like David Bowie, Roxy Music, and The Smiths, formed a band that would eventually be known as Suede (referred to in the transcript as "Swade"). After only a couple of gigs, they quickly achieved "next big thing status." "A bunch of precocious university students stopped listening to their Bowie, Roxy Music and Smith's records long enough to form a group called Swade. A couple of gigs brought them next big thing status."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Historic British Music Paper Cover
podcast.body: This band made history by becoming the first unsigned act to appear on the cover of a British music paper, a significant indicator of their burgeoning impact and critical attention. "eventually they became the first unsigned band to appear on the cover of a British music paper."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Justine Frischmann's Departure and Relationships
podcast.body: The band initially formed with Brett Anderson and Justine Frischmann. Frischmann later left Suede to form Elastica, another significant Britpop band. This was compounded by her becoming romantically involved with Damon Albarn (Blur) after her relationship with Brett Anderson ended, creating considerable tabloid fodder. "Justin Fisherman dejaría Bret Anderson para ser pareja de Damon Alband."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Label Contract Confusion
podcast.body: Suede signed a record contract with the independent label Nude Records, remaining with them until the label eventually closed. However, there was often confusion because Sony had a distribution agreement with Nude Records for Suede's material, as the band's potential for global sales was deemed too large for an independent label to handle alone. Sony and Geffen (described as a major player in the grunge movement) both attempted to sign Suede directly but were unsuccessful, as Suede's rights and freedoms lay solely with Nude. "Sony tenía un acuerdo de distribución con New Records para el material de Swade."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Managed by Ricky Gervais
podcast.body: The Britpop band Suede was, for a brief period, managed by comedian Ricky Gervais. "And comedian Ricky Gervais was for a very brief time the manager of the Britpop band, Swade."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Musical Nationalism
podcast.body: The band intentionally evoked memories of classic British rock from the early 1970s, featuring Jagger Swagger, Glam guitars, and Brett Anderson's dandy English fop persona and proud London accent. This approach carved a distinct niche for them and had undeniable appeal. "It was musical nationalism that had some undeniable appeal."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Producer Shared with Pulp
podcast.body: Suede's first albums were produced by Ed Buller, who later worked with Pulp at Gift Records, marking the beginning of Pulp's progressive success. "Palt's success begins when they manage to sign with Gif Records, which is an independent record label, but that would mark the beginning of Palt's progressive success, when they sign with Gif Records and begin to work with Ed Buller, the producer who had made the first Suede albums."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Resistance to Britpop's Demise
podcast.body: Having entered the Britpop scene relatively late and being "fresh" compared to other bands, Suede was among those who resisted the death of Britpop more than others. They continued to release material, facing a complicated career path afterward, including changing producers, but still produced good albums. "fueron los que un poco más se resistieron a la muerte del beat-pop, me refiero así, al final sacó el vigiarnao y a partir de ahí pues bueno entre una lenta y tortura, a veces un tanto agonía acabó cambiando el productor, bueno llevó una carrera un tanto complicada a partir de ahí aunque nos sacó malos discos."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: El BRIT POP como negocio discográfico

podcast.title: Signing with Nude Records
podcast.body: Suede signed with the independent label Nude for a precise amount of 3,132 pounds, marking a crucial step in their career. "They eventually signed with an indie label called Nude, for exactly 3,132 pounds."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Slow Exit from Britpop
podcast.body: Suede struggled significantly to transition out of the Britpop movement, finding themselves "stuck" as the genre waned. Their later albums, such as *Head Music* (1999), were critically good but released too late to capitalize on the Britpop trend, while *New Morning* (2002), though not Britpop, still contained elements that failed to convince critics, illustrating their slow and difficult adaptation to a post-Britpop landscape. "su salida de Britpop fue muy lenta, muy tardy, ahí les costó muchísimo."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Smiths Influence and Successor Hype
podcast.body: Suede were openly fans of The Smiths, specifically their singer-lyricist and guitarist dynamic. The British music press, eager for a successor to The Smiths, heavily hyped Suede, giving them cover stories before they even released a single. "The British music press hungry for someone to succeed the Smiths. We're all over Swade, giving them cover stories before they even released a single."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: Struggle to Exit Britpop
podcast.body: Suede was identified as one of the bands that experienced significant difficulty in transitioning out of the Britpop movement following its peak. This challenge mirrored Oasis's struggles in adapting their established sound to the evolving musical trends of the late 1990s. "a Wossis le pasó un poco más oíd que les costó fue de las bandas que más les costó salir de movimiento gripo."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Stylistic Evolution
podcast.body: Suede, similar to Blur and Pulp, underwent various stylistic shifts in their early career. Following a strong debut album, they moved towards a more intellectual and glam-influenced sound, shaped by artists like David Bowie and Scott Walker, before fully embracing their Britpop identity. "Swade y el primer disco que es muy grande, después he ido al dogma estar intelectual, después se metió en el V-pop."

xref.title: Britpop's First Couple
xref.body: Frontwoman Justine Frischmann's relationships were a major media focus; she was a former member of Suede, a former girlfriend of Brett Anderson, and the current girlfriend of Damon Albarn of Blur, leading the media to declare them Britpop's "official first couple." "Britpop now had an official first couple."

xref.body: Bowie was a significant acknowledged influence on the emerging Alt Rock stars of the 1990s, including bands like the Pixies, Nirvana, The Smashing Pumpkins, Suede, Oasis, and Blur, which helped introduce his earlier work to a new generation of fans. "The new Alt Rock stars of the 90s constantly acknowledged Bowie as a major influence."

xref.title: Post-Smiths Careers and Lawsuit
xref.body: After The Smiths disbanded, Mike Joyce played with bands like Badly Drawn Boy and Suede. Andy Rourke worked as a hired gun before reuniting with Mike in Vinnie Peculiar. In 1996, both sued Morrissey and Marr for non-payment of royalties. Andy settled for £80,000, while Mike was awarded £1.2 million, which Morrissey has continually appealed. "In 1996, both of them sued Morrissey and Mar for non-payment of royalties."
